source_title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) decision-making process visibility, traceability and compliance governance - ISED Canada
source_excerpt:
From: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada
Shared Services Canada (SSC) is interested in solutions that provide visibility into AI decision-making processes, enhance the traceability of AI outputs, and ensure that AI models comply with the Federal Government's AI Strategy and its Guiding Principles.
Challenge sponsor: Shared Services Canada (SSC)
Closing date: December 22, 2026 14:00 Eastern time

The Government of Canada (GoC) is committed to the responsible use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) compliant with its AI Strategy and Guiding Principles, see references noted in this challenge notice.
The widespread adoption of AI technologies has created opportunities to enhance decision-making and improve service delivery within the GoC. In fostering the responsible usage of AI, the GoC has established an adoption strategy and guiding principles. To support adherence and implementation, the GoC is interested in testing solutions that provide visibility into AI decision-making processes, enhance the traceability of AI outputs, and ensure that AI models comply with Canadian laws and international standards and best practices.
Despite the availability of AI governance solutions from Canadian companies and international providers, existing offerings typically require significant manual effort. This effort is particularly evident in interpreting evolving AI governance requirements, applying them to specific AI systems, updating controls and assessments, and identifying their ecosystem-wide impacts.
The challenge seeks innovation to advance capabilities for identifying and incorporating evolving governance requirements, determining their potential impact on registered AI systems, associated controls, assessments, and evidence, and supporting timely reassessment, all while maintaining explainability, traceability, auditability, and human oversight.
Support the continuous alignment of registered AI systems with relevant Canadian regulations, policies, directives, and other governance requirements and be able to identify potentially affected systems and indicate when a reassessment is required.
Demonstrate interoperability with enterprise systems, Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) platforms and governance solutions and the solution can be integrated with minimal customization. Demonstrate the ability to exchange governance information with enterprise systems and AI/ML lifecycle tools through standards-based Application Programming Interfaces (APIs), connectors and interoperable data exchange mechanisms. Governance information may include AI system metadata, risk assessments, compliance findings, audit evidence, monitoring results, approvals and decision records. As an example: This governance information includes but is not limited to, information about the AI system, ownership, intent, deployment status, funding state, client information, system objectives, assessments, algorithmic impact assessment, control requirements (playbooks). Demonstrate how governance information can be collected, aggregated and maintained across multiple systems through APIs, connectors and data exchange mechanisms. Leverage open standards and documented interfaces to reduce dependency on proprietary technologies enabling interoperability across diverse enterprise environments.

Generate governance reports, alerts, and notifications and integrate with enterprise collaboration, communication, and ticketing/case management systems.
As SSC expands the use of AI solutions, including generative and Agentic AI, there is a growing need for a consistent, centralized, and scalable approach to AI governance. Current governance activities may rely on separate processes, manual tracking, and fragmented documentation, which can limit real-time visibility into AI system inventories, risk posture, compliance status, policy alignment, and decision-making evidence.
Multiple contracts could result from this Challenge.
The maximum funding available for any Phase 2 contract resulting from this challenge is: $2,000,000.00 CAD excluding applicable taxes, shipping, travel and living expenses, as required
The maximum duration for any Phase 2 contract resulting from this challenge is up to 20 months (excluding submission of the final report)
Estimated number of Phase 2 contracts: 1-2
This disclosure is made in good faith and does not commit Canada to award any contract for the total approximate funding. Final decisions on the number of Phase 2 awards will be made by Canada on the basis of factors such as evaluation results, departmental priorities and availability of funds. Canada reserves the right to make partial awards and to negotiate project scope changes.
Note: Selected companies are eligible to receive one contract per phase per challenge.
Solution proposals can be submitted by a business that meets all of the following criteria:
incorporated in Canada (federally or provincially)
small and medium sized business with 499 or fewer full-time equivalent (FTE) employees **
research and development activities that take place in Canada
50% or more of its annual wages, salaries and fees are currently paid to employees and contractors who spend the majority of their time working in Canada Footnote **
50% or more of its FTE employees have Canada as their ordinary place of work Footnote **
50% or more of its senior executives (Vice President and above) have Canada as their principal residence Footnote **
